title: Domains and Ranges of Radical Sum and Product Functions
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: Given the radical functions f(x) = sqrt(x + 1) and g(x) = sqrt(x - 1), find the natural domains and ranges of f, g, the sum f + g, and the product f * g.
finalAnswer: D_f = [-1, \infty),\ R_f = [0, \infty);\quad D_g = [1, \infty),\ R_g = [0, \infty);\quad D_{f+g} = [1, \infty),\ R_{f+g} = [\sqrt{2}, \infty);\quad D_{f\cdot g} = [1, \infty),\ R_{f\cdot g} = [0, \infty)

steps.title: Find the Domains and Ranges of f and g Individually
steps.explanation: For f(x) = sqrt(x + 1), we require x + 1 >= 0, so x >= -1; as x varies over [-1, infinity), sqrt(x + 1) covers [0, infinity). For g(x) = sqrt(x - 1), we require x - 1 >= 0, so x >= 1, and sqrt(x - 1) also covers [0, infinity).
steps.why: A square root function sqrt(x - c) has natural domain [c, infinity) and range [0, infinity).

steps.title: Compute the Common Domain of f + g and f * g
steps.explanation: Intersecting the domain [-1, infinity) of f with the domain [1, infinity) of g gives [1, infinity). Note that even though sqrt(x^2 - 1) is real for x <= -1, the product (f * g)(x) = sqrt(x + 1) * sqrt(x - 1) is only defined where both f(x) and g(x) are individually defined.
steps.why: By definition of pointwise function operations, the domain of f + g and f * g is the intersection D_f cap D_g.

steps.title: Determine the Range of the Sum f + g
steps.explanation: On [1, infinity), both sqrt(x + 1) and sqrt(x - 1) are continuous and strictly increasing. Thus (f + g)(x) attains its minimum at x = 1 with value sqrt(2), and increases without bound as x -> infinity.
steps.why: A continuous strictly increasing function on [1, infinity) that is unbounded above has range [f(1), infinity).

steps.title: Determine the Range of the Product f * g
steps.explanation: For x >= 1, (f * g)(x) = sqrt(x^2 - 1) is continuous and strictly increasing. At x = 1, (f * g)(1) = 0, and as x -> infinity, sqrt(x^2 - 1) -> infinity, giving the range [0, infinity).
steps.why: As x ranges over [1, infinity), x^2 - 1 ranges over [0, infinity), so its principal square root ranges over [0, infinity).
